clue.text: Pollution detected in a Channel Islands sewer

blocks.note: taken as written
CI is the standard abbreviation for the Channel Islands
a sewer is a large underground drain

explanation.surface: An environmental inspector finds contamination in a sewer on Jersey or Guernsey.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sewer' reads as the place the pollution was found, but it is simply a synonym supplying the last chunk. The Channel Islands are British islands off the coast of France.
explanation.definitionFit: Rain made acidic by industrial emissions of sulphur and nitrogen oxides is a well-known form of environmental damage.

clue.text: Content to name a downland field

indicators.note: the content of something is what sits inside it, so the letters wanted lie inside the following words

blocks.note: runs across the end of the first word, the middle word and the start of the third

explanation.surface: Someone is happy to christen a field on the chalk hills of southern England.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Content' looks like the adjective meaning satisfied, but it is the noun: the contents of the phrase. Downland is the rolling grassy chalk country of southern England.
explanation.definitionFit: A grassy stretch of open land, often kept for hay or grazing, is a straightforward synonym for a field.

clue.text: Burns, say, not charged and without penalty

blocks.note: Robert Burns, the national poet, is an example of a native of Scotland
something not charged for costs nothing

explanation.surface: A suspect accused of arson is released without charge or punishment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Burns' looks like injuries or arson, but with 'say' it is Robert Burns, the Scottish poet, as an example. 'Not charged' then shifts from legal to money sense.
explanation.definitionFit: To get away with something scot-free is an idiom for escaping all punishment or harm.

clue.text: Curse a broken piece of crockery

indicators.note: a broken thing is in pieces, so the letters before it are scattered and rearranged

blocks.note: the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone swears at a cup's companion that has just smashed on the floor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Curse' looks like the verb of the person dropping the crockery; it is just letters to shuffle together with the A.
explanation.definitionFit: The small shallow dish placed under a cup is one of the standard items in a tea service.

clue.text: Moves slowly and carefully and steals all but the first

indicators.note: keeping everything except the opening letter means the first letter is dropped

blocks.note: to pinch is informal for to steal

explanation.surface: A burglar creeps cautiously through a house, taking everything except the first item.
explanation.walkthrough: Pinch is everyday British slang for steal; removing its first letter leaves the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: To inch along is an idiom for creeping forward a tiny distance at a time with great caution.

clue.text: Values of current offers

blocks.note: I is the symbol for electric current in physics
deals are offers made in business or shops

explanation.surface: A shopper weighs up what this week's special offers are actually worth.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Current' reads as 'present-day', but it is electrical current, whose symbol is I. 'Values' means principles, not prices.
explanation.definitionFit: Ideals are the moral principles or standards a person holds, which is one everyday sense of values.

clue.text: Masses of water wrecked canoes

indicators.note: a wrecked object has been smashed apart, so the following letters are rearranged

blocks.note: the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Huge waves have smashed some small boats.
explanation.walkthrough: Read 'Masses of water wrecked canoes' as a news headline; the definition is the first three words.
explanation.definitionFit: The great bodies of salt water covering most of the planet are described plainly here as enormous quantities of water.

clue.text: I snore badly, getting older

indicators.note: done badly means done wrongly, so the letters come out in a muddled order

blocks.note: the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone admits their snoring has got worse with age.
explanation.walkthrough: The confession sounds personal, but 'I snore' is just six letters to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: Senior is an adjective describing someone higher in age, as in a senior citizen or the elder of two.

clue.text: Founding it on units it assembled

indicators.note: assembling means putting parts together into a new arrangement

blocks.note: the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Instructions for building flat-pack furniture: base it on the units once put together.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Founding' reads as part of the instructions, but it is the definition, and 'assembled' marks every other word as fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: The act of setting up or establishing something new can be called its institution, as in the institution of a rule.

clue.text: To be manipulated in conversation is necessary

indicators.note: conversation is spoken, so the word is judged by its sound rather than its spelling

blocks.note: kneaded means worked and pressed with the hands, as dough or a stiff muscle

explanation.surface: Being talked round, or manipulated, in a discussion is sometimes unavoidable.
explanation.walkthrough: The silent K means kneaded and the answer sound identical.
explanation.definitionFit: Something required or essential is described as needed, an everyday adjectival use of the past participle.

clue.text: Becoming aware of frost having melted?

blocks.note: first meaning: spotting or perceiving something
second meaning, read as two words: once frost melts there is no longer any icy coating

explanation.surface: Someone realises with surprise that the overnight frost has thawed.
explanation.walkthrough: Split the answer into two words, NOT ICING: melted frost is no longer icing. The question mark flags that playful split.
explanation.definitionFit: To notice something is to perceive it, so the participle means coming to perceive or observe it.

clue.text: This jumper could really make you itch!

definitions.text: This jumper could really make you itch!

blocks.clueFragment: This jumper could really make you itch!
blocks.note: surface reading: a scratchy woollen sweater, which the British call a jumper
setter's reading: a tiny leaping insect whose bites cause itching

explanation.walkthrough: In British English a jumper is a sweater, and coarse wool is famously itchy; but the jumper meant is a parasite that leaps.
explanation.definitionFit: This small wingless insect is known for its huge jumps and for bites that leave the skin itching.

clue.text: Irrigate grounds to keep dry?

definitions.note: verb sense: to make something impervious to water

blocks.note: to irrigate land is to supply it with water
grounds for believing something are evidence

explanation.surface: A groundskeeper is told to water the lawns, oddly in order to keep them dry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Grounds' looks like land to be watered, but it means reasons or evidence. The question mark acknowledges the paradox of watering to stay dry.
explanation.definitionFit: To waterproof something is to treat it so that rain cannot get in, preventing it from becoming wet.

clue.text: It could be a local number

definitions.text: It could be a local number

blocks.clueFragment: It could be a local number
blocks.note: surface reading: a nearby telephone number, or a song by a local band
setter's reading: a numbing drug, of the kind a dentist injects into one area only

explanation.walkthrough: 'Number' is not the counting word but something that numbs; a local is the type that deadens one part of the body.
explanation.definitionFit: A drug that causes loss of sensation, given to a small area for minor surgery, is literally something that numbs.

clue.text: Shut up, dear, interrupting final...

indicators.note: to interrupt is to break in, so one piece is placed inside another

blocks.note: the final part of something is its end
a dear friend is a close friend

explanation.surface: Someone tells their partner to be quiet just as the cup final is about to begin.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shut up' sounds like a rude command, but it means confined, as animals shut up in a pen.
explanation.definitionFit: Something shut up is confined or fenced in, which is what the past participle means here.

clue.text: Designed to be fashionable and well maintained

blocks.note: what is in is in fashion
a well-kept garden has been tended

explanation.surface: A garden or a car built both to look stylish and to be kept in good order.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Designed' looks like part of a description of a stylish object, but it is the definition in the sense of meant.
explanation.definitionFit: Something designed for a purpose is meant or planned to do it, the sense of 'intended to'.

clue.text: Roundabout entertainment

blocks.note: first meaning: a circular road junction, as in London's Piccadilly or Oxford one
second meaning: a travelling show of acrobats, clowns and animals

explanation.walkthrough: A roundabout is also a fairground ride, which tempts toward the fair; but here it is a traffic junction. In British place names such a junction is called this, as in Piccadilly.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names both a circular open space where streets meet and a show performed in a ring under a big top.

clue.text: Strength is concealed by keener gymnasts

indicators.note: something concealed is tucked away inside, so the wanted letters sit within the following words

blocks.note: runs from inside the first word into the start of the second

explanation.surface: Enthusiastic gymnasts hide how powerful they really are.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters straddle the gap between the two words.
explanation.definitionFit: Vigour or power to act is a common synonym; both describe the capacity for physical effort.

clue.text: Slipped broken coils into outmoded frame

indicators.note: a broken thing is in pieces, so these letters are scattered and rearranged
putting one thing into another places it inside
a frame surrounds what it holds, so one piece forms the outside

blocks.note: the letters to be rearranged
outmoded things are out of date

explanation.surface: An old-fashioned bed frame has some snapped springs slipped into it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Slipped' looks like part of the repair story, but it is the definition, as in a slipped disc or joint.
explanation.definitionFit: A bone that has slipped out of its normal position at a joint is described as put out of place.

clue.text: Myth associated with the German songs

blocks.note: a myth is a widely held falsehood
der is a German word for the

explanation.surface: A legend linked with traditional German songs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The German' is a common device for one of the German articles; the definition is plural to match.
explanation.definitionFit: Lieder are German art songs, typically for voice and piano, by composers such as Schubert; the word is the plural.

clue.text: Eliminate certain features of Hindi spelling

indicators.note: some features of a thing are parts of it, so the wanted letters are a part of the following words

blocks.note: runs from the end of the first word into the second

explanation.surface: A teacher wants to get rid of some quirks of how Hindi is written.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Certain features of' sounds like linguistics, but just marks that part of the next two words is wanted.
explanation.definitionFit: To drive away doubts or fears is to get rid of them completely, a close synonym of removing.

clue.text: Can you start to get tiddly?

indicators.note: the start of a word is its opening letter

blocks.note: a tin is a can
the first letter of the word

explanation.surface: A question asking whether you can begin to get slightly drunk.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tiddly' usually means tipsy, which the surface uses, but it is also British informal for very small.
explanation.definitionFit: Tiddly is a British colloquial word for very small, alongside its better-known sense of slightly drunk.

clue.text: Image of Christ in church house concealed by extremely eccentric doctor

indicators.note: the extremes of a word are its two outermost letters
something concealed is hidden inside, so it is enclosed by other pieces

blocks.note: the first and last letters of the word
CE is the Church of England
HO is the abbreviation for house
MO is a medical officer, an army doctor

explanation.surface: A religious painting is hidden in a church building by an odd doctor.
explanation.walkthrough: The outer pair and the doctor together form the shell around the church and house abbreviations.
explanation.definitionFit: Ecce Homo, Latin for 'behold the man', is the title of many paintings showing Christ crowned with thorns before Pilate.

clue.text: Several dehydrate in the open, perhaps

blocks.note: first meaning: various, assorted
second meaning, read as one hyphenated verb: dry food by leaving it out under the sun

explanation.surface: A few people suggest drying something outdoors.
explanation.walkthrough: The second half describes sun-drying, as with tomatoes; 'perhaps' admits the hyphenated verb is a slightly different form.
explanation.definitionFit: Sundry is an adjective meaning various or of different kinds, as in 'all and sundry' or sundry items.

clue.text: Appeared to be joined in speech

indicators.note: speech is heard rather than read, so the word is judged by its sound

blocks.note: seamed means joined with a seam, as in sewing

explanation.surface: Two people looked as though they were united in what they said.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Appeared to be joined' reads as one phrase, but 'to be' only links the definition to the sound-alike.
explanation.definitionFit: To seem is to give the impression of being something, so the past tense matches the verb 'appeared'.

clue.text: In this place, spout your primarily unorthodox opinions

indicators.note: primarily means first of all, so only the opening letters are kept

blocks.note: here means in this place
the first letters of these two words

explanation.surface: An invitation to air your controversial views right here.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spout' looks like the verb governing the opinions, but it only gives its first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Heresy is belief contrary to accepted doctrine, especially religious; a set of such dissenting views fits.
